description: TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition: the ADM phases, content framework and deliverables, Enterprise Continuum, techniques, governance and business architecture. For enterprise architects preparing for TOGAF certification or using the ADM at work.

notes.front: What structural change defines the TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition, compared with 9.2?
notes.back: It became modular: stable Fundamental Content plus a flexible TOGAF Library of Series Guides. The core Architecture Development Method (ADM) stayed largely the same.
notes.extra: Why: guidance (Agile, Digital, Security...) can evolve without re-issuing the core standard.

notes.text: Of the four architecture domains in The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) (Business, Data, Application, Technology), {{c1::Data}} and {{c2::Application}} together form the {{c3::Information Systems Architectures}} developed in Phase C.

TOGAF 10 Fundamental Content documents: Introduction and Core Concepts · {{c1::Architecture Development Method (ADM)}} · {{c2::ADM Techniques}} · {{c3::Applying the ADM}} · {{c4::Architecture Content}} · {{c5::Enterprise Architecture Capability and Governance}}.

notes.front: In TOGAF, what are the two meanings of "architecture"?
notes.back:
1. A formal description (detailed plan) of a system to guide its implementation
  2. The structure of components, their interrelationships, and the principles governing their design and evolution

notes.front: Per TOGAF, why does an enterprise need Enterprise Architecture?
notes.back: To turn a fragmented legacy of processes and systems into an integrated environment that responds to change and supports the business strategy.
notes.analogy: EA is city planning: individual buildings (projects) still get designed, but zoning and shared infrastructure keep the city coherent as it grows.

notes.text: Architecture Development Method (ADM) phases in order: Preliminary → A {{c1::Architecture Vision}} → B {{c2::Business Architecture}} → C {{c3::Information Systems Architectures}} → D {{c4::Technology Architecture}} → E {{c5::Opportunities & Solutions}} → F {{c6::Migration Planning}} → G {{c7::Implementation Governance}} → H {{c8::Architecture Change Management}}.

notes.front: Why is Requirements Management drawn at the centre of the Architecture Development Method (ADM) rather than as a numbered phase?
notes.back: It is continuous: every phase both feeds requirements into and draws them from the requirements repository.
notes.analogy: It is the hub of a wheel: each spoke (phase) connects to it, none owns it.

notes.front: Does the Architecture Development Method's (ADM's) Requirements Management process itself prioritise or resolve requirements?
notes.back: No. It identifies, stores and routes requirements; prioritising and addressing them happens in the relevant phases.

notes.text: Architecture Development Method (ADM) iteration cycles: Architecture Capability ({{c1::Preliminary + A}}) · Architecture Development ({{c2::B–D}}) · Transition Planning ({{c3::E–F}}) · Architecture Governance ({{c4::G–H}}).

notes.front: In the Architecture Development Method (ADM), Baseline vs Target Architecture: what is the difference, and what links them?
notes.back: Baseline = as-is; Target = to-be. The gap between them drives the work packages in the Architecture Roadmap.

notes.front: Objective of the Architecture Development Method (ADM) Preliminary Phase?
notes.back: Prepare the organisation to do enterprise architecture (EA): establish the Architecture Capability (tailor the framework, define Architecture Principles, choose tools, set up governance).
notes.extra: Answers "where, what, why, who and how we do architecture".

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase A: Architecture Vision?
notes.back: Set scope, stakeholders and constraints, create a high-level aspirational vision of the value to be delivered, and get the Statement of Architecture Work approved.
notes.extra: Phase A is the project initiation of an architecture cycle. Input: Request for Architecture Work.

notes.front: In TOGAF, what is a Business Scenario and in which phase is it typically used?
notes.back: A technique that describes a business problem, its actors, and the desired outcome, to discover real requirements. Typically used in Phase A.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase B: Business Architecture?
notes.back: Develop the Target Business Architecture (how the enterprise must operate to reach its goals and the Vision) and identify gaps from the Baseline.

notes.front: What does Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase C cover, and in what order?
notes.back: The Information Systems Architectures: Data and Application Architecture, in either order or in parallel.

notes.front: In Phase C, what is the Data Architecture concerned with (and not concerned with)?
notes.back: The types and sources of data the business needs: data entities, described stably and completely. Not database design.

notes.front: In Phase C, what does the Application Architecture define?
notes.back: The major kinds of application systems needed to process the data and support the business, as logical groups of capability, independent of products.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase D: Technology Architecture?
notes.back: Define the target logical and physical technology components (hardware, software, networks, platforms) that host the application and data components.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions?
notes.back: Produce the initial complete Architecture Roadmap, identify delivery vehicles (projects, programs), and decide whether Transition Architectures are needed.
notes.extra: First phase directly concerned with implementation.

notes.front: What is a Transition Architecture?
notes.back: A formal description of the architecture at a point in time between Baseline and Target: an intermediate state that delivers business value incrementally.
notes.analogy: Like the stable intermediate floors when renovating a building you still live in: each one must be habitable.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase F: Migration Planning?
notes.back: Finalise the Architecture Roadmap and the Implementation and Migration Plan, prioritising work packages by cost/benefit and risk, aligned with portfolio and change management.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase G: Implementation Governance?
notes.back: Architectural oversight of implementation: ensure delivery projects conform to the Target Architecture.

notes.front: Which TOGAF document binds development partners and sponsors to the architecture during implementation?
notes.back: The Architecture Contract: a joint agreement on deliverables, quality and fitness for purpose, used to govern compliance.

notes.front: Objective of Architecture Development Method (ADM) Phase H: Architecture Change Management?
notes.back: Keep the architecture lifecycle current: manage changes to the architecture and decide whether a change needs a new ADM cycle.

notes.front: In Phase H, when does a change trigger a new Architecture Development Method (ADM) cycle rather than an incremental change request?
notes.back: When it has broad, strategic impact across many stakeholders. Changes that fit the existing architecture are handled incrementally.

notes.front: TOGAF Content Framework: deliverable vs artifact vs building block?
notes.back:
• Deliverable: contractually specified, formally reviewed and signed off
  • Artifact: granular work product (catalog, matrix, diagram)
  • Building block: reusable component of capability
notes.extra: Deliverables contain artifacts; artifacts describe building blocks.

notes.front: ABB vs SBB: what is the difference?
notes.back: An Architecture Building Block specifies required capability, vendor-neutral (the what). A Solution Building Block is the concrete product or component that implements it (the how).
notes.analogy: ABB = "a relational database with point-in-time recovery"; SBB = "PostgreSQL 16 on managed service X".

notes.text: TOGAF artifact types: {{c1::catalogs}} list building blocks; {{c2::matrices}} show relationships between them; {{c3::diagrams}} render them visually.
notes.extra: Examples: Technology Standards Catalog, Business Interaction Matrix, Business Footprint Diagram.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Architecture Content Metamodel?
notes.back: A model of the types of building blocks (entities) in an architecture and the relationships between them, so content is classified and stored consistently.

notes.front: What makes a good TOGAF building block?
notes.back: A package of functionality meeting business needs, with published interfaces, loosely coupled so it is reusable and replaceable.

notes.front: What is the Request for Architecture Work, and what does it trigger?
notes.back: A document from the sponsoring organisation asking for architecture work to start. It triggers Phase A.

notes.front: What is the Statement of Architecture Work, and when is it approved?
notes.back: The scope and approach of an architecture project: its work plan/contract. Approved in Phase A.

notes.front: Request for Architecture Work vs Statement of Architecture Work: who writes which?
notes.back: The Request comes from the sponsor and starts the engagement. The Statement is the architecture team's response defining scope and plan, approved in Phase A.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the Architecture Vision deliverable?
notes.back: A high-level, aspirational summary of the change, created early (Phase A) to win stakeholder buy-in before detailed work starts.
notes.analogy: The architect's sketch shown to the client before any blueprints are drawn.

notes.front: What does the Architecture Definition Document (ADD) contain?
notes.back: The core architecture artifacts and narrative, Baseline and Target, across all four domains. It is qualitative.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS)?
notes.back: The quantitative, measurable requirements the architecture must meet.

notes.front: Architecture Definition Document (ADD) vs Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS): how do they differ?
notes.back: The ADD describes the architecture (qualitative: models and narrative). The ARS states measurable requirements a solution must meet (quantitative). They are companions.

notes.front: What is the Architecture Roadmap, and where is it built?
notes.back: Work packages laid out on a timeline from Baseline to Target. Started in Phase E, finalised in Phase F.

notes.front: What is the Implementation and Migration Plan, and in which phase is it finalised?
notes.back: The schedule for implementing the Roadmap, coordinated with enterprise change management. Finalised in Phase F.

notes.front: What is the Capability Assessment deliverable used for?
notes.back: Assessing current and target capability (business, IT, architecture maturity) to understand readiness and gaps. Created in Phase A, used in Phase E.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Communications Plan?
notes.back: A Phase A deliverable defining which stakeholders get what information, how often and by which channel.

notes.front: What is the Tailored Architecture Framework, and where is it produced?
notes.back: TOGAF (plus any other frameworks) adapted to the enterprise: method, content and principles. Produced in the Preliminary Phase, refined in Phase A.

notes.front: What is the Compliance Assessment deliverable?
notes.back: A Phase G record of how far a project's implementation conforms to the architecture, with deviations and any dispensations.

notes.front: What is the Enterprise Continuum?
notes.back: A classification of repository content from generic to organisation-specific. It comprises the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum.
notes.analogy: A library shelved from general textbooks to your own company's manuals: you start generic and specialise.

notes.text: Levels of both the Architecture and the Solutions Continuum, generic → specific: {{c1::Foundation}} → {{c2::Common Systems}} → {{c3::Industry}} → {{c4::Organization-Specific}}.

notes.front: What does each of the Architecture Continuum and the Solutions Continuum hold, and how are they linked?
notes.back: The Architecture Continuum holds specifications (Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs)); the Solutions Continuum holds implementations (Solution Building Blocks (SBBs)). Each architecture level guides the matching solutions level.

notes.front: How does the Architecture Development Method (ADM) use the Enterprise Continuum as it progresses?
notes.back: The architect moves generic → specific: reuses Foundation/Common/Industry assets and feeds new Organization-Specific architectures back into the repository.

notes.text: The TOGAF Architecture Repository holds: the {{c1::Architecture Metamodel}}, {{c2::Architecture Capability}}, {{c3::Architecture Landscape}}, {{c4::Standards Information Base}}, {{c5::Reference Library}}, {{c6::Governance Log}} and {{c7::Architecture Requirements Repository}}.

notes.front: What are the three levels of the TOGAF Architecture Landscape?
notes.back:
• Strategic: long-term, enterprise-wide summary
  • Segment: a portfolio or business area
  • Capability: a specific capability/solution to deliver
notes.analogy: Map zoom levels: country → region → street.

notes.front: What is the Standards Information Base (SIB)?
notes.back: The repository part holding the standards new architectures must comply with (legal, industry, organisational) and conforming products.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Governance Log?
notes.back: The repository record of governance activity: decisions, compliance assessments, dispensations and contracts. An audit trail.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM)?
notes.back: A Foundation Architecture: a taxonomy of generic platform services and the application platform.

notes.front: What problem does the III-RM (Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model) address?
notes.back: Boundaryless Information Flow: integrated information access across the enterprise. It is derived from the Technical Reference Model (TRM), focused on application software.

notes.front: What is a Foundation Architecture in TOGAF?
notes.back: The most generic level of the Architecture Continuum: generic services and functions (e.g., the Technical Reference Model (TRM)) on which more specific architectures build.

notes.text: A TOGAF Architecture Principle has four parts: {{c1::Name}}, {{c2::Statement}} (the rule), {{c3::Rationale}} (business benefit) and {{c4::Implications}} (impact of adopting it).
Quality criteria for a set of Architecture Principles: {{c1::Understandable}}, {{c2::Robust}}, {{c3::Complete}}, {{c4::Consistent}}, {{c5::Stable}}.

notes.front: What does Gap Analysis identify in the Architecture Development Method (ADM), and where is it applied?
notes.back: For each building block: retained, eliminated or new, so nothing is accidentally omitted. Applied in Phases B, C and D.
notes.extra: Pitfall it catches: a Baseline service that is eliminated without anyone intending it.

notes.front: What is Capability-Based Planning for?
notes.back: Planning and delivering strategic business capabilities across functions, bridging strategy and project delivery.

notes.front: What does the Business Transformation Readiness Assessment evaluate, and when?
notes.back: The organisation's preparedness for change, using readiness factors, to expose transformation risks. Used in Phases A and E.

notes.front: TOGAF risk management: initial vs residual risk?
notes.back: Initial: before mitigation. Residual: after mitigating actions.
notes.extra: Impact derived from effect × frequency; tracked in a Risk Register.

notes.front: In TOGAF, what is interoperability, and its three common categories?
notes.back: The ability to share information and services. Categories: operational/business, information, technical.

notes.front: What is Architecture Partitioning, and why do it?
notes.back: Dividing the enterprise architecture (EA) by subject (breadth), detail (depth), time and maturity to manage complexity and assign teams. It underpins Strategic/Segment/Capability levels.

notes.front: What is a Stakeholder Map (power/interest grid) used for?
notes.back: Classifying stakeholders by power and interest to choose engagement: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.

notes.front: Why use Architecture Alternatives and Trade-offs in the Architecture Development Method (ADM)?
notes.back: To compare candidate architectures on requirements, principles, cost, risk and value, making the Target choice explicit and justifiable.

notes.front: Why is security treated as cross-cutting in the Architecture Development Method (ADM) rather than as a phase?
notes.back: Security and risk requirements affect every domain and phase, so security guidance threads through the whole cycle.

notes.front: What is Architecture Governance?
notes.back: The practice by which enterprise architectures are managed and controlled enterprise-wide: governance framework, compliance and control of work products.

notes.front: What is the role of the Architecture Board?
notes.back: A cross-organisation body that oversees implementation: ensures consistency, manages compliance and dispensations, and makes governance decisions.

notes.text: TOGAF compliance levels, least to most aligned: {{c1::Irrelevant}} → {{c2::Consistent}} → {{c3::Compliant}} → {{c4::Conformant}} → {{c5::Fully Conformant}}; any of them with features implemented contrary to the spec is {{c6::Non-conformant}}.

notes.front: TOGAF compliance: Compliant vs Conformant?
notes.back: Compliant: not all spec features implemented, but everything implemented follows the spec. Conformant: all spec features implemented per spec, plus extra features outside it.
notes.extra: Consistent: only some features in common, plus extras. Fully conformant: exact correspondence.

notes.front: What is a dispensation in architecture governance?
notes.back: A time-bound, recorded exemption for a project that cannot yet comply, with conditions and an expiry date.
notes.analogy: A temporary building permit variance: allowed for now, with a deadline to fix it.

notes.text: Characteristics of good governance in TOGAF: {{c1::Discipline}}, {{c2::Transparency}}, {{c3::Independence}}, {{c4::Accountability}}, {{c5::Responsibility}} and {{c6::Fairness}}.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Architecture Capability Framework for?
notes.back: Establishing and operating the architecture function: roles, skills, governance structures and the Architecture Board.

notes.front: What is the TOGAF Architecture Skills Framework?
notes.back: A definition of roles, skills and proficiency levels for architects, used to assess and develop the architecture capability.

notes.front: What is an Architecture Maturity Model used for?
notes.back: Benchmarking the maturity of the architecture practice (process, governance, skills) to show where it must improve. Usually CMM-style.

notes.text: The four foundational TOGAF Series Guides for Business Architecture: {{c1::Business Capabilities}}, {{c2::Value Streams}}, {{c3::Organization Mapping}} and {{c4::Information Mapping}}.

notes.front: In TOGAF Business Architecture, what is a business capability?
notes.back: A particular ability the business has to achieve a purpose: what it does, independent of how, who or where. Stable over time.

notes.front: In TOGAF Business Architecture, what is a value stream?
notes.back: An end-to-end sequence of value-adding stages that produces a result for a customer, stakeholder or end user.

notes.front: Business capability vs value stream: how do they relate?
notes.back: A capability is a stable ability (what); a value stream is a sequence of stages delivering value. Capabilities enable value-stream stages; cross-mapping shows which capabilities matter for which value.
notes.analogy: Capabilities are the instruments in an orchestra; a value stream is the piece being played, calling on instruments in order.

notes.front: What does Organization Mapping show in TOGAF Business Architecture?
notes.back: Organisational units, partners and stakeholders related to capabilities and value streams: who delivers value.

notes.front: What does Information Mapping link, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Business information to capabilities and value streams. It is the bridge from Business Architecture to Data Architecture.

notes.front: List every Architecture Development Method (ADM) phase after the Preliminary Phase in order, with its one-line purpose.
notes.back:
1. A Vision: scope and value
  2. B Business: target business operation
  3. C Data and Application
  4. D Technology
  5. E Opportunities & Solutions: roadmap and delivery vehicles
  6. F Migration Planning: prioritised plan
  7. G Implementation Governance: conformance oversight
  8. H Change Management: keep it current

notes.front: Why does the Architecture Development Method (ADM) develop Business Architecture (Phase B) before Data, Application and Technology?
notes.back: Business goals and processes determine what data, applications and technology are needed. Starting with technology risks building systems that do not serve the business.

notes.front: A new requirement appears during Phase D of the Architecture Development Method (ADM). What happens to it, and what breaks if the process is skipped?
notes.back: Requirements Management records it in the requirements repository and routes it to the affected phases for assessment. Skipped, earlier phases' work silently becomes inconsistent with the new need.

notes.front: When are Transition Architectures worth creating, and what is the risk without them?
notes.back: When the gap between Baseline and Target is too large to deliver in one step. Without intermediate states, value arrives only at the very end and risk concentrates in one big-bang change.

notes.front: What can go wrong if Phase A of the Architecture Development Method (ADM) ends without an approved Statement of Architecture Work?
notes.back: Scope, approach and stakeholder commitment are undefined, so later phases risk scope creep and disputes over what the architecture work was meant to deliver.

notes.front: A vendor product is swapped for another that meets the same capability. Which changes: the Architecture Building Block (ABB) or the Solution Building Block (SBB)?
notes.back: Only the SBB changes. The ABB (required capability, vendor-neutral) stays valid, which is why separating the two makes solutions replaceable.

notes.front: In Gap Analysis, how is a building block classed if it is in the Baseline but absent from the Target, and if it is in the Target but absent from the Baseline?
notes.back: In Baseline only: eliminated. In Target only: new (to be developed or procured). In both: retained.

notes.front: An implementation delivers every feature the specification requires, correctly, plus extra features outside it. What is its TOGAF compliance level?
notes.back: Conformant. Compliant would mean only some spec features are implemented (those that are follow the spec).

notes.front: A project cannot meet an architecture standard before its deadline. What mechanism lets it proceed without silently breaking governance?
notes.back: A dispensation: a recorded, time-bound exemption with conditions and expiry, logged in the Governance Log and reviewed by the Architecture Board.

notes.front: Why must an Architecture Principle include Rationale and Implications, not just a Statement?
notes.back: Rationale explains the business benefit, so people accept the rule. Implications expose the cost of following it, so it can be debated and applied consistently. A bare rule is easily ignored or argued away.

notes.front: A company reorganises its departments but keeps doing the same things. Which Business Architecture elements stay stable, and which change?
notes.back: Business capabilities stay stable (they describe what the business does, not who). Organization Mapping changes, because it links units to capabilities and value streams.

notes.front: Why does Information Mapping help the move from Business Architecture to Data Architecture?
notes.back: It identifies the business information each capability and value stream needs, which becomes the data entities that the Data Architecture describes.
